title: Impact of Short Sale Ban on Financial Stock Volatility

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy

**Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID)**

This is a classic DID setup: we have financial stocks subject to a short selling ban (treated) and stocks not subject to the ban (control), observed before and after the ban implementation. The interaction term `treat_x_post` is already constructed, capturing the DID estimator.

**Key Assumptions:**
1. **Parallel trends**: In the absence of the ban, treated (financial) and control (non-financial) stocks would have followed similar trends in log volatility.
2. **No contemporaneous shocks**: No other policy or event differentially affected financial vs. non-financial stocks at the same time as the ban.
3. **SUTVA**: The ban on short selling of financial stocks did not spill over to affect the volatility of non-financial stocks.

The coefficient on `treat_x_post` identifies the causal effect of the short sale ban on log stock volatility.

## 2. R Code

```r
# =============================================================
# Impact of Short Sale Ban on Financial Stock Volatility (DID)
# =============================================================

library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# Load data
df <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s43_data.csv")

cat("=== Data Overview ===\n")
str(df)
cat("\nDimensions:", nrow(df), "x", ncol(df), "\n")
cat("\nSummary:\n")
print(summary(df))

# Check treatment/control and pre/post composition
cat("\n=== Treatment-Period Cross-Tab ===\n")
print(table(Treated = df$treated, Post = df$post))

# Group means
cat("\n=== Group Means ===\n")
group_means <- aggregate(y ~ treated + post, data = df, FUN = mean)
print(group_means)

# Manual DID calculation
mean_treat_post <- mean(df$y[df$treated == 1 & df$post == 1])
mean_treat_pre  <- mean(df$y[df$treated == 1 & df$post == 0])
mean_ctrl_post  <- mean(df$y[df$treated == 0 & df$post == 1])
mean_ctrl_pre   <- mean(df$y[df$treated == 0 & df$post == 0])

did_manual <- (mean_treat_post - mean_treat_pre) - (mean_ctrl_post - mean_ctrl_pre)
cat("\n=== Manual DID Estimate ===\n")
cat("Treated Pre:  ", round(mean_treat_pre, 4), "\n")
cat("Treated Post: ", round(mean_treat_post, 4), "\n")
cat("Control Pre:  ", round(mean_ctrl_pre, 4), "\n")
cat("Control Post: ", round(mean_ctrl_post, 4), "\n")
cat("DID Estimate: ", round(did_manual, 4), "\n")

# ---- Model 1: Basic DID regression ----
cat("\n=== Model 1: Basic DID Regression ===\n")
model1 <- lm(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post, data = df)
print(summary(model1))

# Robust standard errors (HC1)
cat("\n=== Model 1 with Robust (HC1) Standard Errors ===\n")
robust_se1 <- coeftest(model1, vcov = vcovHC(model1, type = "HC1"))
print(robust_se1)

# ---- Model 2: With unit fixed effects ----
cat("\n=== Model 2: DID with Unit Fixed Effects ===\n")
df$unit_id_f <- as.factor(df$unit_id)
model2 <- lm(y ~ unit_id_f + post + treat_x_post, data = df)
cat("DID coefficient (treat_x_post):\n")
print(summary(model2)$coefficients["treat_x_post", ])

# Robust SE for model 2
robust_se2 <- coeftest(model2, vcov = vcovHC(model2, type = "HC1"))
cat("\nWith robust SE:\n")
idx <- which(rownames(robust_se2) == "treat_x_post")
print(robust_se2[idx, ])

# ---- Model 3: With unit and period fixed effects (if multiple periods) ----
n_periods <- length(unique(df$period))
if (n_periods > 2) {
  cat("\n=== Model 3: Two-Way Fixed Effects ===\n")
  df$period_f <- as.factor(df$period)
  model3 <- lm(y ~ unit_id_f + period_f + treat_x_post, data = df)
  cat("DID coefficient (treat_x_post):\n")
  print(summary(model3)$coefficients["treat_x_post", ])
}

# ---- Key Result Summary ----
cat("\n========================================\n")
cat("       KEY RESULT SUMMARY\n")
cat("========================================\n")
coef_did <- coef(model1)["treat_x_post"]
se_did <- robust_se1["treat_x_post", "Std. Error"]
p_did <- robust_se1["treat_x_post", "Pr(>|t|)"]
cat(sprintf("DID Estimate (Short Sale Ban Effect): %.4f\n", coef_did))
cat(sprintf("Robust Std. Error:                    %.4f\n", se_did))
cat(sprintf("p-value:                              %.4f\n", p_did))
cat(sprintf("95%% CI: [%.4f, %.4f]\n", coef_did - 1.96*se_did, coef_did + 1.96*se_did))
cat(sprintf("Significant at 5%%? %s\n", ifelse(p_did < 0.05, "YES", "NO")))
cat("========================================\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings

**Expected sign: Negative** – The DID coefficient on `treat_x_post` is expected to be negative, indicating that the short sale ban **reduces** log stock volatility for treated (financial) stocks relative to controls.

**Expected magnitude:** A reduction in log volatility on the order of -0.3 to -0.8 would be plausible, though the empirical literature is actually mixed on this. Some studies (e.g., Beber & Pagano, 2013) find that short sale bans **increase** volatility or have no beneficial effect, in which case we might see a positive or insignificant coefficient.

**Rationale:** The stated research question frames the ban as potentially reducing volatility — the policy rationale being that short sellers amplify downward price pressure. However, short sellers also contribute to price discovery and liquidity, so removing them could increase volatility. The DID design cleanly identifies this effect by comparing financial stocks (banned) to non-financial stocks (not banned) around the ban implementation, netting out common time trends and permanent group differences.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in log stock volatility between treated and untreated stocks before and after the ban.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The short selling ban led to a reduction in log stock volatility for the treated financial stocks.
